triage_context.environment: Internet-facing web service (HTTP is untrusted). Identity.API, WebApp and the mobile BFF are externally exposed; internal service hops are a lower-trust boundary but still reachable after a foothold.
threat_model: Denial of service against a paid SLA
triage_context.scoring: Derived HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW from preconditions and access level

findings.title: Catalog write endpoints (POST/PUT/DELETE) are completely unauthenticated and reachable through the external mobile BFF
preconditions: External reachability to the mobile BFF
A trivially supplied api-version query value
A target item id, freely enumerable from the public GET list
findings.threat_match: DoS against paid SLA; catalog integrity
findings.rationale:
CatalogApi.cs:100,105,110,114 map PUT/POST/DELETE with no RequireAuthorization, and Catalog.API registers no authentication or authorization middleware (Program.cs). AppHost.cs:63 makes the mobile BFF externally reachable and Extensions.cs:142 forwards /api/catalog/{*any} for all methods with no auth or method restriction; the handlers persist attacker data via SetValues/Add/Remove. An unauthenticated internet client can create, reprice or delete catalog items.

Zero meaningful preconditions: the BFF is internet-facing, the route is method-agnostic, and Catalog.API registers no auth, so any anonymous client can create, reprice or delete items using ids the public GET enumerates. Mass deletion is a direct availability attack and price rewriting is a financial-fraud primitive that propagates over the event bus. Textbook unauthenticated-remote HIGH; the claim is well calibrated.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Mike Kistler (3 of 3 recent commits); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: RSA token-signing private key committed to the repository and used as the live signing credential
preconditions: Read access to the repo or a published artifact (the key is committed)
Knowledge of the issuer URL and a target sub, both public/derivable
Network reach to the API surface
findings.rationale:
tempkey.jwk:1 contains full RSA private parameters (D/P/Q/DP/DQ/QI, HasPrivateKey true) and Identity.API.csproj:50 copies it to output. Program.cs:37 unconditionally loads it via AddDeveloperSigningCredential while Program.cs:29 disables key management, so it is the live non-rotating issuer key; .gitignore does not exclude it. APIs trust the matching JWKS with ValidateAudience=false (AuthenticationExtensions.cs:33-49), so anyone with the repo can forge tokens for orders/basket/webhooks.

The committed file is a genuine 2048-bit RSA private key, loaded unconditionally with key management disabled, so the deployed IdP signs with a publicly known key. APIs trust that issuer with audience validation off and authorize purely on sub, so anyone can mint tokens for any user. Unauthenticated remote account takeover and cross-user order/PII access; HIGH is warranted, though it is not RCE or true admin escalation.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Aditya Mandaleeka (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Any authenticated customer can ship any order
preconditions: A valid authenticated principal (no role needed)
A target order number, trivially enumerable
The order must already be Paid
The api-version query value for the external route
findings.rationale:
PUT /api/orders/ship is gated only by bare RequireAuthorization (Program.cs:21-22) with no role or policy, and ShipOrderCommandHandler.cs:21-27 loads and ships whichever order number the body supplies. The handler comment says ship is an administrator action, yet no admin role exists, and the external BFF forwards /api/orders/* (Extensions.cs:146) so any customer token can ship a victim's Paid order and block cancellation.

Ship is protected by bare authentication and the handler ships whatever order number the body supplies, with no role, buyer or tenant check, despite being documented as an administrator action. Any customer can invoke an admin business function against arbitrary paid orders, permanently blocking cancellation or refund. Two preconditions plus the admin-escalation threat match land on HIGH.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Rob Conery (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Received-webhook token column is rendered to unauthenticated visitors
preconditions: The home page is anonymous (no [Authorize], plain RouteView, no fallback policy)
At least one webhook delivery has occurred
Validation enabled for the leaked token to be a working bypass
findings.rationale:
ReceivedMessages.razor:13 renders hook.Token, and Home.razor:22 invokes it outside the AuthorizeView on the anonymous / route; Routes.razor uses plain RouteView and no fallback policy exists. The token is the captured X-eshop-whtoken used as the shared delivery secret, and the gated RegisteredHooks column shows it was meant to be hidden. Anonymous visitors can read it after a legitimate delivery.

The token column renders outside the AuthorizeView on the anonymous home page, so any visitor can read the shared delivery secret and the serialized order PII in the Data column. Zero preconditions at unauthenticated access maps to HIGH; the PII threat match would raise it further if it were not already at the ceiling. The claimed MEDIUM understates it.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Steve Sanderson (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Unauthenticated /add-webhook page renders the configured webhook validation token into the HTML
preconditions: Network reach to WebhookClient
Knowing the predictable /add-webhook route
Server-side prerendering active (the default)
findings.rationale:
AddWebhook.razor:1 exposes /add-webhook with no [Authorize], and OnInitialized copies WebhookClientOptions.Token into an input that is emitted during prerender. The token is the configured X-eshop-whtoken secret used by WebhookEndpoints and WebhooksSender, and Home.razor:11 shows the UI intended the area to be login-gated. Validation being off by default lowers impact but does not make the disclosure intentional.

The page has no [Authorize] and prerenders the configured webhook validation token into an input, so a single unauthenticated GET harvests the exact X-eshop-whtoken secret. Possession enables forged deliveries whenever validation is enabled. The 0-precondition/unauthenticated-remote rule lands it at HIGH, one band above the claimed MEDIUM, though the default-off validation tempers marginal gain.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Steve Sanderson (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: JWT bearer disables audience validation, so any token from the IdP is accepted by every API
preconditions: A valid IdP-signed token for a different audience (self-registration plus a secretless client suffices)
The target resource requires no additional scope check
findings.rationale:
AuthenticationExtensions.cs:40 sets the per-service audience but :49 disables ValidateAudience, and all three consumers gate with policy-less RequireAuthorization. The IdP defines disjoint orders/basket/webhooks resources, so a webhooks-audience token or a client ID token is accepted by Ordering and mapped via sub. The claimed cross-user impact depends on separate IDOR findings, but cross-audience token replay is real and reachable.

Audience validation is disabled and every consumer uses policy-less RequireAuthorization, so a token issued for basket or webhooks is accepted by Ordering. Base severity is MEDIUM for the authenticated requirement, but the PII/cross-tenant impact is directly reachable once admitted, raising it one step to HIGH. Claimed severity matches.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Michael Stonis (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Any authenticated user can cancel any other user's order
preconditions: A valid authenticated account
A target order in a cancellable state
A target order number, trivially enumerable
A non-empty x-requestid GUID
findings.rationale:
CancelOrderAsync forwards a body-supplied order number to CancelOrderCommandHandler.cs:21, which loads the order by id and calls SetCancelledStatus with no comparison to the caller's sub. The only gate is authentication, the validator checks only non-zero, and HiLo-sequential ids are enumerable. The listing path proves per-user scoping is intended, so any authenticated user can cancel another buyer's not-yet-paid order.

Cancel loads the order purely by body-supplied number and calls SetCancelledStatus with no comparison to the caller's sub, so any authenticated buyer can cancel another buyer's not-yet-paid order. Impact is unauthorized state change with no PII read or admin escalation. One or two preconditions at authenticated access maps to MEDIUM; the claim is accurate.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Rob Conery (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: GET /api/orders/{orderId} returns any order without an ownership check
preconditions: A valid authenticated identity with the orders scope
A valid order id, trivially enumerable from HiLo-sequential ints
A target order that exists
findings.rationale:
OrdersApi.cs:84 passes the raw route id to OrderQueries.cs:6-10, which filters only on o.Id and returns the full shipping address and items. The group gate is authentication only, no ownership policy or query filter exists, and order ids are HiLo-sequential. The sibling listing path filters by Buyer.IdentityGuid (OrderQueries.cs:40), proving ownership scoping was intended but omitted here.

GetOrderAsync filters solely on id and returns full shipping address and items, while the only gate is authentication, so any customer can read every other buyer's order by walking sequential ids. It is a genuine cross-buyer confidentiality break with real PII and is trivially automatable, but it requires an authenticated scope-bearing account and is read-only. HIGH overrates an authenticated IDOR by one step.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Srushti (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Full PAN and CVV are written to logs on order creation, and CVV is logged by every MediatR behavior
preconditions: A valid authenticated account
An explicit empty-GUID x-requestid header
Warning-level logging enabled and logs retained/forwarded
A reader not entitled to card data
findings.rationale:
OrdersApi.cs:134 logs the raw CreateOrderRequest record, whose generated ToString prints the full CardNumber and CardSecurityNumber, and it fires before the masking at line 140. Any authenticated client can trigger it with a zero GUID x-requestid; the code comment at line 130 shows logging the request contradicts intent. The CVV also passes unmasked into CreateOrderCommand, which is logged at lines 148-153 and in IdentifiedCommandHandler.cs:79-84, with no redaction filter.

Line 134 serializes the whole CreateOrderRequest record, PAN and CVV included, before the masking at line 140, so any caller supplying an empty request GUID forces plaintext card data into logs. It stays at MEDIUM because the endpoint is authenticated, the logged values are attacker-supplied, and disclosure needs retained logs readable by an unauthorized party. PCI-relevant, but not admin, RCE or cross-tenant; HIGH is one step high.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Rob Conery (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Order item prices and quantities are accepted from the client request, allowing arbitrary order totals
preconditions: A valid authenticated token
Calling POST /api/orders directly rather than through the repricing WebApp
Product ids with sufficient stock
findings.rationale:
The request body binds a client-controlled item list; BasketItemExtensions.cs:20-21 copies UnitPrice and Quantity verbatim, CreateOrderCommandHandler.cs:44 persists them, and Order.GetTotal derives the total from them. The validator only checks non-emptiness and OrderItem permits unitPrice 0/0.01; no catalog or basket re-fetch exists. The trusted WebApp re-prices server-side (BasketState.cs:141), confirming prices should not come from the client.

UnitPrice and Quantity flow unchanged into the persisted order item and total, with only a non-empty check and no catalog or basket re-fetch. An authenticated buyer can set an arbitrary total. Two preconditions at authenticated access maps to MEDIUM; the payment step is simulated, and no threat-model entry is implicated.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Aditya Mandaleeka (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: CreateOrder trusts body-supplied UserId instead of the JWT sub claim
preconditions: A valid authenticated token
For a specific victim, knowledge of their sub GUID
findings.rationale:
CreateOrderAsync builds the command from body-supplied request.UserId (OrdersApi.cs:141) while IIdentityService is injected but unused; no validator or policy supplies the missing check. The value becomes Buyer.IdentityGuid and the OrderStartedIntegrationEvent UserId, which Basket.API uses to delete /basket/{UserId}. The external /api/orders route makes this reachable by any authenticated client, enabling order-history poisoning and cross-user basket deletion.

CreateOrder copies body-supplied UserId into the command while IIdentityService is unused, so the token identity is never consulted. That value becomes the buyer identity and the OrderStarted event UserId that Basket uses for deletion, giving cross-user integrity impact. It is not unauthenticated and exposes no victim data back to the attacker, so it stays at the authenticated MEDIUM tier.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Rob Conery (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Webhook signing token written to logs in cleartext at Information level
preconditions: A valid authenticated account on Webhooks.API
Read access to or compromise of the OTLP log backend
The caller is the subscription creator whose own token is logged
findings.rationale:
GrantUrlTesterService.cs:17 and :25 log the caller and expected webhook tokens verbatim at Information, reached live from WebHooksApi.cs:41. The token is the shared X-eshop-whtoken credential used by WebhooksSender.cs:24 and validated at WebhookEndpoints.cs:37. Logs default to Information and are exported formatted via OTLP (ServiceDefaults/Extensions.cs:54,87-93) with no redaction, so log readers can harvest the secret and forge deliveries.

The caller and expected tokens are logged verbatim at Information and exported over OTLP, so with endpoint configured the secret leaves the process into a shared store. Two preconditions place it at MEDIUM; exposure becomes cross-user only when the log backend is compromised, and the token grants no admin access, PII or RCE. Claimed MEDIUM is correct.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Aditya Mandaleeka (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Authenticated user can force server-side OPTIONS/POST requests to arbitrary hosts
preconditions: A valid authenticated token
Network reach to Webhooks.API (internal-only in the reference topology)
The same-origin check is satisfied by submitting the same internal URL twice
findings.rationale:
WebHooksApi.cs:41 forwards caller-controlled Url/GrantUrl to TestGrantUrl, which sends an OPTIONS request to that host at GrantUrlTesterService.cs:21. The only checks are Uri.IsWellFormedUriString and a same-origin comparison of two attacker-supplied URLs (GrantUrlTesterService.cs:37-45), both trivially satisfied. Service discovery resolves internal Aspire names, no egress allowlist or private-range block exists, and any authenticated shopper can drive the server-side request.

A caller-supplied URL is fetched server-side with service discovery active and no egress restriction, and the same-origin guard is vacuous. Exploitability is constrained: it needs authenticated credentials and sends a bodyless OPTIONS whose only observable is a success/failure oracle. That is authenticated access with 2-3 preconditions, i.e. MEDIUM rather than HIGH, though the second-order stored-webhook POST keeps it from dropping further.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Aditya Mandaleeka (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Persistent blind SSRF: stored DestUrl is POSTed without re-validation and redirects are followed
preconditions: A valid authenticated account
A controlled endpoint that passes the grant handshake
A paid order to trigger delivery
A redirect or DNS rebind to the internal target
findings.rationale:
DestUrl is stored from caller input at WebHooksApi.cs:48 and POSTed verbatim by WebhooksSender.cs:17,32 with no delivery-time validation. The default HttpClient follows redirects (AllowAutoRedirect is never disabled), so a passing endpoint can later 307/DNS-rebind delivery to internal services or metadata. Delivery is triggered by a paid order via OrderStatusChangedToPaidIntegrationEventHandler.cs:16, and only RequireAuthorization gates registration.

DestUrl is stored after a one-time grant check and later POSTed with no delivery-time validation while the default client follows redirects, so a passing host can redirect to internal services. It is a blind SSRF: no response is returned, only an event body and attacker token are sent, limiting exfiltration. Registration requires authentication plus a token-echoing endpoint, so HIGH is overstated by one step.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Aditya Mandaleeka (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Full raw integration-event bodies (buyer name, identity GUID) are written to span tags and logs
preconditions: A running RabbitMQ consumer subscribed to order events
A normal order status transition producing buyer PII
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT set
Read access to the trace store
findings.rationale:
RabbitMQEventBus.cs:157/161 tags every consumed body and line 172 logs it on failure with no redaction, and shipped events carry BuyerName and BuyerIdentityGuid. The bus is live in every service and Warning logs are enabled by default, with formatted OTLP export when configured. Exposure is to log/telemetry readers rather than remote HTTP clients, which keeps it LOW, but the PII data flow is concrete.

Line 161 tags the full raw body of every consumed event before deserialization, shipping BuyerName, BuyerIdentityGuid and UserId to any configured OTLP backend with no redaction. Exploitation needs three-plus preconditions including trace-store access, so it is not HIGH, but the exposure is systematic, persistent PII with long retention and broad telemetry access. Claimed LOW understates it; MEDIUM with a +2 alignment.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: iem365-michael (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Logout failure leaves access/refresh tokens in SecureStorage; post-logout redirect is unregistered
preconditions: A signed-in victim with tokens persisted in SecureStorage
Logout fails (unregistered post-logout redirect or transient IdP/network error)
The caller ignores the false result
Later device or keystore access
A still-valid access or refresh token
findings.rationale:
IdentityService.cs:49-54 returns on LogoutAsync error before the only SetUserTokenAsync(default), and LoginViewModel.cs:107 discards the false result. The client sends maui://authcallback while IdentityServer registers only maui://authcallback/Account/Redirecting (Config.cs:57), so logout predictably errors and the access/refresh tokens remain in SecureStorage; the next launch auto-restores the session. Impact needs device access, but the logout operation is genuinely broken.

The error return precedes the sole token wipe, the caller ignores it, and startup re-authenticates from the surviving token, so logout leaves a live session. Impact is genuine order history, address and card claims, but exploitation needs device access plus a failed logout. Three-plus preconditions and local-only access is LOW before the PII threat match, which raises it one step to MEDIUM.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Michael Stonis (4 of 4 recent commits); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: All confidential OIDC clients share the literal client secret "secret", including the public MAUI client
preconditions: The client secret is public by construction
A valid authorization code or refresh token for a victim (separate capture vector)
Fixed redirect URIs limit re-pointing; maui still requires PKCE
Network reach to the token endpoint
findings.rationale:
Config.cs:52,82,118 register the identical literal secret for maui/webapp/webhooksclient, loaded unconditionally at Program.cs:34 with no override, and the MAUI app ships the same value (SettingsService.cs:15). RequirePkce=true blunts the scheme-hijack chain for maui, but webapp has RequirePkce=false (Config.cs:90) and offline access, so the public secret is the only client-authentication factor for redeeming a captured code or refresh token. Live credential, though the demo context lowers severity.

The hardcoded, client-shipped secret is confirmed and unmitigated, with RequirePkce=false on webapp, so client authentication at the token endpoint is genuinely defeated for three clients. Severity is capped below HIGH because the Code-only grant means the secret alone yields no token; exploitation is contingent on independent code capture against a fixed redirect. Real defense-in-depth collapse that needs a concrete code-capture path to confirm.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Michael Stonis (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: GET /Account/Logout signs the user out without a prompt, enabling logout CSRF
preconditions: A victim with a live session cookie who issues a top-level GET to /Account/Logout
ShowLogoutPrompt stays false (the global default)
findings.rationale:
ShowLogoutPrompt=false (AccountOptions.cs:12) makes the anonymous GET handler call the POST logout overload directly at AccountController.cs:156, bypassing the [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] filter at line 166, and SignOutAsync runs at line 175. SameSite=Lax still sends the cookie on a cross-site top-level GET, so a malicious page can force sign-out. Impact is limited to session denial, but the mechanism is concrete.

The antiforgery bypass is real: the GET handler invokes the POST action in-process, so a bare top-level GET signs out any authenticated user and Lax still ships the cookie. But the only capability gained is forced logout, a session-availability nuisance with no data exposure, privilege escalation or tenant crossing. Classic logout-CSRF; LOW matches the claim.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Aditya Mandaleeka (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Expected webhook token is logged in cleartext on every unauthenticated request
preconditions: Read access to the WebhookClient log sink
Log aggregation or OTLP export enabled
ValidateToken actually effective and the token non-default
findings.rationale:
WebhookEndpoints.cs:35 logs tokenToValidate (the configured secret from line 14) and the caller token at Information before the check at line 37, on every anonymous request. It runs for accepted and rejected requests, and ServiceDefaults formats and OTLP-exports logs with no redaction. Severity is LOW because log access is required, but the cleartext-secret data flow is real.

The log statement runs at Information on every request and can ship the expected token off-box, so the disclosure is real and unmitigated. Monetizing it requires telemetry access, export configured and validation actually enforced, while the token is a low-privilege shared secret already committed in appsettings. Three-plus preconditions and no PII/admin/RCE impact keep it at LOW.
findings.owner_hint: top committer: Steve Sanderson (1 of 1 recent commit); no CODEOWNERS entry

findings.title: Internet-facing mobile BFF catch-all routes forward unauthenticated requests to anonymous Catalog write endpoints
OIDC confidential-client secret `secret` is hardcoded for webapp and webhooksclient
Cross-user basket deletion: OrderStarted deletes the basket of any event-supplied UserId, and the publisher takes it from the request body
OIDC confidential-client secret (`secret`) embedded in the shipped app and stored in plaintext Preferences
CVV, card number and full PII are issued in id_tokens/userinfo to every client
findings.rationale: ProfileService.cs:23 does emit all claims, but the first-party MAUI client deliberately consumes card_number/card_security_number from userinfo (IdentityService.cs:85-88, CheckoutViewModel.cs:61-64), so issuance is the sample's intended profile contract. Claims are scoped to the authenticated sub, all clients are statically registered first-party clients, and seeded card data is masked demo data. No cross-user path or real cardholder data exists.

findings.title: Identity DB seeder re-creates demo users alice/bob with password Pass123$ and the login page advertises it
findings.rationale: UsersSeed.cs:33/78 seed alice/bob with Pass123$, but the credential is deliberately published on the login page (Login.cshtml:46), whitelisted as Dummy in CredScanSuppressions.json, and used by CI. The seeded profile data is masked placeholder data, no role is granted, and README.md:118 scopes the deployment to evaluation/demo. This is intended sample onboarding, not a leaked production secret.

findings.title: Anonymous POST /webhook-received injects arbitrary data into a global store rendered to every visitor
findings.rationale: The anonymous-accept path is explicit at WebhookEndpoints.cs:13,37 (token validation is opt-in and off by default), and the received feed is deliberately public (Home.razor:22). QuickGrid HTML-encodes the payload, so no XSS or privilege change follows; the only effects are demo-feed content spoofing and unbounded queue growth (volumetric DoS). The webhooksclient is also not externally published in the reference topology (AppHost.cs:67).

findings.title: NuGet vulnerability audit warnings globally suppressed
findings.rationale: Directory.Build.props:11 does suppress NU1901-NU1904 under TreatWarningsAsErrors, but NuGet audit still runs and only the warning is hidden. Dependabot independently monitors NuGet (dependabot.yml:7) and versions are centrally pinned; no vulnerable package or exploit path is identified. This is build-time visibility hygiene, not a vulnerability in the running service.

findings.title: Create/Update bind the full CatalogItem entity, allowing overposting of Id, PictureFileName, Price and stock fields
findings.rationale: Binding CatalogItem is the documented request contract (Catalog.API.json:469-473,1075-1143), and the endpoint is the intended catalog CRUD surface; there is no field-level privilege boundary to cross, because Catalog.API has no authentication at all (the real issue is f001). Embedding is [JsonIgnore] (CatalogItem.cs:39) and recomputed at line 392, the body Id is bounded by the identity column, and the cited dead-null and embedding-wipe claims are misreads.

findings.title: Webhook token validation reads the wrong configuration key, so ValidateToken is silently ignored
findings.rationale: The endpoint does read root ValidateToken while the options property is bound but never read, yet the root key is the one the repo's own test exercises and passes (WebhookClientTests.cs:62-73). No shipped configuration sets either key, so validation is off by default regardless, which is the separate open-ingest issue (f015). The mismatch only misleads an operator who picks an undocumented spelling; it creates no new exploit path.

findings.title: CI actions referenced by mutable tags instead of commit SHAs
findings.rationale: Mutable-tag references are present in pr-validation.yml:23,25 and sibling workflows, but all are first-party actions/* in build/test-only jobs with no deploy secrets or production artifacts. Exploitation requires compromising GitHub's action org or the npm registry, not input reachable from this service. The repo already demonstrates SHA pinning in its reference templates; this is CI hygiene, not a concrete vulnerability.

findings.title: webapp confidential client disables PKCE while its client secret is public
findings.rationale: Config.cs:90 does set RequirePkce=false for webapp, but the only consumer is the ASP.NET Core OIDC handler (WebApp/Extensions.cs:77-79), which defaults UsePkce=true and binds codes to a server-held verifier, so a leaked code plus the public secret cannot be redeemed. The handler also never requests offline_access (Extensions.cs:83-86), so the claimed refresh-token impact does not occur. What remains is the separately reported hardcoded secret and a confidential-client hardening choice.

findings.title: Chatbot exposes a PII function tool and renders model-chosen image URLs, enabling prompt-injection exfiltration
findings.rationale: GetUserInfo is exposed only as a model tool (ChatState.cs:43) and returns the current per-circuit user's own claims, so no cross-user PII flow exists. The MarkupString sink HTML-encodes text and both image attributes (MessageProcessor.cs:23-24,28), preventing XSS, and catalog image URLs are rebuilt from an int id. The residual is LLM prompt injection, which is out of scope and returns data only to the victim's own browser.

findings.title: returnUrl filtering in /user/login is bypassable with protocol-relative URLs
findings.rationale: LogIn.razor:6 binds the query returnUrl and line 14 only rejects absolute URIs, so //evil.example can reach NavigateTo. The page is live and linked from UserMenu.razor:25, and [Authorize] only forces an OIDC round trip. But the impact is a post-authentication open redirect with no token or data leak, which rule 12 classifies as a low-impact nuisance.

findings.title: Forwarded-header trust enabled globally clears the trusted-proxy list, allowing X-Forwarded-For/Proto spoofing
findings.rationale: Extensions.cs:36 is the output of Aspire's first-class AddForwardedHeaders API, called at AppHost.cs:6 for the Dev Proxy/Container Apps ingress and asserted by AppHostConfigurationTests.cs:46. The only RemoteIpAddress consumer is the [Authorize] DiagnosticsController.cs:14, which returns the caller's own claims; no auth gate consults IsHttps, and in ACA the ingress-supplied rightmost X-Forwarded-For is the one honored under ForwardLimit=1.

findings.title: BFF and WebApp forward bearer tokens and login credentials over hardwired HTTP to internal services
findings.rationale: Extensions.cs:146/150 target the internal http endpoints of the Aspire-managed BFF, and ordering exposes only an http profile (launchSettings.json). External endpoints default to HTTPS (AppHost.cs:22), plain HTTP is test-only (AppHost.cs:110-117), and ordering/catalog are not externally exposed, so TLS terminates at ingress and the cleartext hop stays inside the private environment. The residual is missing internal mTLS requiring an adjacent-network foothold.

findings.title: Official build pipeline extends a 1ES template from a mutable release tag
findings.rationale: ci.yml:18 uses refs/tags/release, but ci.yml:20 extends the Unofficial 1ES template from a first-party Microsoft-owned internal repo, and retagging requires write access there, outside the untrusted HTTP boundary. The pipeline is build-only with no deploy secrets, and the repo's threat model already records the item as partially mitigated. Pinning a SHA is hardening, not an actionable vulnerability.

findings.title: Production consumer contains a "throw-fake-exception" body trigger that force-fails and drops any event containing it
findings.rationale: The throw-fake-exception check at RabbitMQEventBus.cs:163-166 is an explicit fault-injection hook with a comment saying so, caught at 170 and ACKed at 180. BuyerName can reach event bodies, but only the acting buyer's own name is carried, so the effect is dropping that buyer's own notification. It is deliberate demo behavior with no cross-user or confidentiality impact.

findings.title: Database container pinned to the mutable ankane/pgvector:latest tag
findings.rationale: AppHost.cs:13-14 does use ankane/pgvector:latest and Playwright launches the AppHost, but the image is hardcoded operator configuration with no untrusted-input influence, and README.md:118 scopes the container topology to evaluation/demo use. Postgres is internal-only and the CI job runs on an ephemeral runner. The claimed data volumes do not exist in AppHost.cs; digest pinning is hygiene, not an exploitable path.

findings.title: ATS fully disabled in the Mac Catalyst Release bundle and cleartext globally declared on Android
findings.rationale: The plist key exists, but this is client-app platform config: Android network_security_config.xml:3-5 scopes cleartext to 10.0.2.2, iOS uses only NSAllowsLocalNetworking, and defaults are loopback/emulator addresses with mocks enabled (SettingsService.cs:25). No attacker-reachable cleartext path exists from this config alone; it is local-dev hardening in a sample client, outside the internet-facing service.

findings.title: Gateway endpoints default to plaintext HTTP and have no scheme validation; card PAN/CVV and bearer tokens are POSTed in cleartext
findings.rationale: The http:// defaults resolve only to localhost or the Android emulator alias 10.0.2.2 (SettingsViewModel.cs:16,58,68), explicitly for local emulator development, and the app ships with UseMocksDefault=true (SettingsService.cs:25). The identity endpoint defaults to https, cleartext is scoped to 10.0.2.2, and the gateway URLs are developer-entered settings, so no untrusted network path carries card data or tokens.

findings.title: Order PII is broadcast to every user's subscription of an event type; per-user scoping is stored but not enforced
findings.rationale: GetSubscriptionsOfType does lack a UserId predicate, but this is a topic-based pub/sub fan-out: the UI promises registering a hook lets you see new paid orders (AddWebhook.razor:9) and renders a global feed (Home.razor:20). UserId is enforced for subscription CRUD (WebHooksApi.cs:16,27,72), and the API's shipped event contract omits BuyerIdentityGuid. The attacker creates their own subscription rather than supplying a victim id, so this is not IDOR; only order id/status plus BuyerName are fanned out.

findings.title: OIDC/JWT metadata acquisition is allowed over HTTP, enabling signing-key substitution
findings.rationale: RequireHttpsMetadata=false is real, but it only relaxes a check; key substitution requires an http:// authority. The AppHost defaults to the https launch profile (AppHost.cs:22) and injects that https endpoint as Identity__Url, while the HTTP path is test-only (AppHost.cs:107-116) and the remaining http authorities are localhost dev settings or test fixtures. No deployed configuration disables TLS for metadata, so this is a hardening gap rather than a reachable key-substitution path.

findings.title: ACR build script takes a GitHub PAT as a mandatory command-line argument
findings.rationale: queue-all.ps1:6 takes an operator-typed mandatory PAT and passes it to az acr build-task at line 32; no automated caller exists anywhere in the repo, so no HTTP-reachable path supplies or observes the value. The exposure is inherent to a CLI credential flag on the operator's own machine, a local artifact rather than an internet-facing vulnerability. This is a trusted operator/CLI input.

findings.title: Loopback-only diagnostics gate can be satisfied with a spoofed X-Forwarded-For header
findings.rationale: DiagnosticsController is [Authorize] (line 8), so the loopback check at line 14 is defense-in-depth and a spoofed X-Forwarded-For only shows an authenticated caller their own claims and cookie properties. The enabling cause is the global forwarded-header trust already reported as f032, and a standalone deployment without the AppHost env var retains loopback-only proxy trust. Same root cause and same fix; at most low-impact hardening.

findings.title: WebhookClient /login returnUrl is passed to NavigateTo after only a UriKind.Relative parse
findings.rationale: ReturnUrl from the query is parsed with UriKind.Relative and passed to NavigateTo, so //evil.example resolves cross-origin; no local-URL or host allowlist exists, and [Authorize] is inert because Routes.razor uses RouteView. But this is a plain open redirect with no token or code in the URL, which rule 12 classifies as a low-impact nuisance; the WebhookClient is also not externally exposed (AppHost.cs:67).

findings.title: Webhook validation shared secret committed in appsettings.json
findings.rationale: The GUID is only compared when root ValidateToken is true, and no config sets that key, so it is never enforced by default. It is the subscriber's own choice, prefilled into a public form (AddWebhook.razor:30), echoed to the sender, rendered in the UI and logged, and WebhookClient is internal-only (AppHost.cs:67). The actionable defect is the disabled/mis-keyed validation (f024), not the committed demo value.

findings.title: Integration events are dispatched on the unauthenticated routing key; any publisher can forge any event
findings.rationale: Line 192 is a lookup against a closed allowlist of registered event types, not an authentication check, and the routing key at publish time is the server-side CLR type name (line 33) from internally constructed events. RabbitMQ has no external endpoint (AppHost.cs:10) and requires broker credentials, so forging an event presupposes a compromised adjacent workload (T20). Missing signing/vhosts/TLS is hardening, not an internet-reachable flaw.

findings.title: Debug HTTP handler disables TLS validation with a forgeable issuer-name check
findings.rationale: The weak certificate callback exists only inside #if DEBUG and #if ANDROID, and no csproj or CI build defines DEBUG for Release, so release artifacts never register the handler and fall back to default validation. It is a localhost dev shim in the MAUI client, not the internet-facing service; the iOS branch is explicitly scoped to https://localhost.

findings.title: Consumer ACKs messages even when processing throws, silently discarding failed or injected events
findings.rationale: The unconditional ACK at line 180 is real, but lines 177-179 explicitly document it as a deliberate sample simplification without a DLX, and failures are logged with the payload at line 172 rather than erased. Triggering it requires broker write access, which already permits event forgery, and the only HTTP-reachable throw path duplicates f036. The residual is reliability hardening.

findings.title: Implicit grant enabled with AllowAccessTokensViaBrowser for three swagger clients
findings.rationale: The three implicit clients exist, but the only OAuth UI is Scalar, mapped only in Development (OpenApi.Extensions.cs:26-41), and the registered redirect /swagger/oauth2-redirect.html has no handler anywhere in the repo since Swashbuckle is absent. IdentityServer only returns fragments to the exact registered URI, so no reachable page receives a token; the code's own TODO (OpenApiOptionsExtensions.cs:176) marks this as deprecated-flow debt.

findings.title: Exported activity accepts the unverified custom scheme maui://authcallback and the callback URL is hardcoded
findings.rationale: The exported activity is the MAUI-mandated custom-scheme callback, and the redirect URI comes from OidcClient settings rather than attacker input. The maui client requires PKCE (Config.cs:56) and OidcClient validates state/nonce, so a co-registered handler receives an unredeemable code and forged callbacks are rejected. The residual gap is unverified scheme vs App Links, i.e. hardening.

findings.title: Session cookie uses sliding expiration with no absolute lifetime and default Secure/SameSite policy
findings.rationale: Line 71 leaves the framework-default sliding ExpireTimeSpan on a configurable 60-minute session, which only matters after a cookie is already stolen. SaveTokens is required because HttpClientExtensions.cs:40 reads access_token from the ticket, and no offline_access is requested, so no refresh token is persisted; HTTPS redirection and HSTS (Program.cs:21,26) keep the cookie Secure in deployment. What remains is hardening advice (absolute lifetime, explicit Secure/SameSite).

findings.title: OIDC metadata fetching over plaintext is permitted for the WebApp and WebhookClient
findings.rationale: RequireHttpsMetadata=false is real at WebApp:82 and WebhookClient:58, but it only permits an http authority; the AppHost injects the https identity endpoint by default (AppHost.cs:22,30,79), and http is selected only by the test-only ESHOP_USE_HTTP_ENDPOINTS switch (AppHost.cs:107-116). WebhookClient is not externally exposed. The same sinks are already reported as f041, making this a duplicate missing-hardening note.

findings.title: OpenAPI documents are mapped in every environment and may be reachable through the BFF
findings.rationale: MapOpenApi is outside the IsDevelopment guard and the OpenApi section ships in base config, but the affected services have no external endpoints (only identity, webapp and mobile-bff are external). WebApp forwards only product images and the BFF routes are prefix-scoped, with no demonstrated dot-segment path to /openapi. The Catalog schema is already a public checked-in artifact, so no confidential disclosure results.

findings.title: Payment outcome is a fixed configuration flag with no order, amount or idempotency validation
findings.rationale: The handler is a documented payment-gateway simulator (lines 15-19) driven by the operator-controlled PaymentSucceeded flag. PaymentProcessor exposes no HTTP endpoint, so the only trigger is an internal RabbitMQ event requiring broker access, and downstream SetPaidStatus only transitions from StockConfirmed with an idempotency wrapper. This is intended reference-app design, not an internet-reachable flaw.

findings.title: Deployment workflow templates pipe a remote script to bash while holding id-token: write
findings.rationale: The cited YAML is a reference template inside .github/skills, not a workflow under .github/workflows; GitHub Actions never executes it. Its only inbound reference is a documentation link, and none of the real workflows contain curl|bash or id-token: write. No OIDC-enabled job runs this file, so the described exposure does not exist in an executing form.

findings.title: Anonymous semantic-search text is forwarded unbounded to the external embedding provider and logged verbatim
findings.rationale: The text binds from the path or query string, so Kestrel's default 8 KB request-line limit bounds it; no MaxRequestLineSize override exists. The embedding provider is off by default and enforces its own token cap, and the text is logged only at Trace/Debug while the default level is Information. What remains is the absence of a rate limit/quota, already recorded as availability gap T23 and excluded as volumetric hardening.

findings.title: Hybrid Blazor client hardcodes a cleartext HTTP BFF base address in all build configurations
findings.rationale: MobileBffHost resolves only to localhost or the Android emulator host-loopback alias 10.0.2.2, so traffic never crosses an interceptable network. The only data on that client is public catalog JSON and images, with no auth handler or token anywhere in HybridApp, and Android cleartext is narrowed to 10.0.2.2. The BFF is a local Aspire dev resource, making this deliberate local-dev configuration.

findings.title: Same-origin product-image proxy will serve attacker-named SVG files with image/svg+xml
findings.rationale: The proxy and .svg MIME mapping are real and PictureFileName is anonymous-writable, but the handler serves only files that already exist under Pics, which contains only seeded .webp images. No upload or file-write path exists anywhere, and the PhysicalFileProvider blocks traversal, so an attacker cannot place an SVG on disk. Rendering through also blocks script execution, leaving only MIME/header hardening.

findings.title: AddDefaultAuthentication fails open when the Identity section is missing
findings.rationale: The early return is deliberate optional-auth behavior, documented by the inline comment, and all callers ship an Identity section in appsettings with AppHost injecting Identity__Url; a missing Url throws via GetRequiredValue. Reaching the branch requires an operator to strip configuration, and skipping AddAuthorization does not fail open when UseAuthorization runs (startup throws). This is a design/hardening note, not an attacker-reachable bypass.

findings.title: Full card number (PAN) persisted in cleartext in ordering.paymentmethods
findings.rationale: OrdersApi.cs:140 masks the PAN to all-X except the last four digits before CreateOrderCommand is built, and that masked value is the only one flowing through Order, the OrderStarted handler and Buyer.VerifyOrAddPaymentMethod into the mapped CardNumber column. No alternate path persists a raw PAN, so the column only ever holds a masked number, which is intentional PCI-safe minimization.
